messages.subject: GNU public license and using R to migrate / improve upon an excel-based model
messages.subject_clean: GNU public license and using R to migrate / improve upon an excel-based model
messages.body_plain:
Dear davis-ruggers,

I am planning to convert / upgrade a Jurassic excel-based behemoth for database spreadsheets and computational model into R for my work. This database and model has for the past decade or so been sold to various companies for the service of maintaining and updating the database and integrating new capabilities into the model. Now that some of the companies funding the work have younger employees, they are pushing for the work to be migrated to more sensible software.

My question concerns the GNU public license versions 2 and 3. Assuming I write a series of scripts (eventually a package) to reproduce and build upon the current model capabilities, and assuming I'd like to use many of the most useful libraries available (which are themselves licensed mostly under GNU public licenses), will my employer continue to be able to charge its client companies to access not only the database, but also the package that I develop?

Under what conditions would this be viable without violating the GNU public license, and respecting not only the letter but also the spirit of the license?

Thanks in advance for your help,
Jacob Teter
UCD graduate, 2015

messages.body_plain:
Jacob,

Private companies write and sell private R packages all the time.  My understanding is that the key distinction is that your R package *links to* R and other packages, but *does not include code from them.* You and your company are not reusing, modifying, or distributing the code from your dependencies (and R itself) that are GPL-licensed,  so it's fine that your private, commercial package depends on them.  It would be a different story if you, say, copied code from those other packages to include in yours.  Then you would be obligated to follow the terms of GPL which require you to release your code under a compatible share-alike license.

I'm always wary when I wade into these discussions on licenses, as they can be complex and I'm no expert.  But I'm sure someone will point out where I'm wrong :)

Noam

Hi Jacob & Noam,

here's a not-irrelevant stackexchange Q&A:

https://opensource.stackexchange.com/questions/4414/if-my-r-package-uses-gpl-packages-does-mine-automatically-inherit-gpl

I'm not 100% sure I understand the details, but here's my 2c:

* if you distribute GPL licensed packages in any way shape or form, you MUST
  include access to the source code of those packages;

* if you distribute software that includes GPL licensed code (i.e. your R
  package?) you must also make the source code available for all the software
  that depends on that GPL licensed code.  This is the contaminatory aspect of
  GPL.

I'm not a lawyer, tho, and that's pretty much who you need to talk to about
this.

cheers,
--titus

Hi folks,

This week we will have another presentation, this time on how to use RMarkdown for a number of things (CV, reports, presentations, etc). Rich Pauloo will give a tutorial and overview of this tool, so please come join us at tomorrow at 10am, in the DSI (360 Shields) <http://dsi.ucdavis.edu/directions.html>. We will screen cast the event via youtube, so you can watch the presentation live or later (HERE <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CHBOVuo6RCo>) if you can't make it. I'll post any materials Rich provides on the website as well.

Upcoming Presentations:

Nov 16: Kate Tiedman:  using raster /raster calculations in R
Nov 30: Ryan Peek: mapmaking with R/RStudio

PACKAGE OF THE WEEK:

Currently there are 11, 712 total packages on CRAN <https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/>. This week a package I'd like to put out in the ether is cowplot <https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/cowplot/index.html>. It makes it pretty easy to grid or arrange multiple ggplots, and make very nice polished figures for manuscripts or publishing wherever. Plenty of great options within the package. Check it out.

Do you have a package you really enjoy using? Please send it/them my way! Here's a google form we can use to compile all of these: https://goo.gl/forms/VzzeldnaEOkNImJ73.

If you want to see the packages that I've mentioned thus far this quarter, there's a table here <https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/e/2PACX-1vQH6BvP8p-YZOWpYFVIJYBa8AyscYgQB0Mone8NUKhlwKAA8UfGmUoIy22CO1AHOkNTR3Q4LSu2lvVm/pubhtml>.

Thanks much,
Adios,
Ryan

>
>> "By default, shinyapps.io <http://shinyapps.io> deploys all applications on ‘medium’ instances,
> which are allowed to use 512 MB of memory.....shinyapps.io <http://shinyapps.io> does not make
> any guarantees regarding the number of CPU cores, or the speed of the CPUs
> that are allocated to the deployed applications."
>
> My guess is that shinyapp.io <http://shinyapp.io> is spinning up small Amazon or other cloud
> instances when applications fire up, and they're grabbing whatever the
> lowest-cost instance is that's available, which could be of varied number
> of cores or memory.  If you specify more cores than are available, it'll
> work, but you'll be using up memory resources you don't need to by copying
> the objects in memory into different processes.  It's possible that for
> your larger, more complex shapefiles you are hitting memory limits as a
> result, and those processes are failing so you are only getting back a
> subset of the results.  If you just use lapply() it might be slow, but
> you'll be more likely to get all the results back.
>
> Unless you're using Shiny on high-power servers, you'll probably have

> *fewer* resources in the cloud than on your machine. Even the Pro accounts

> for shinyapps.io <http://shinyapps.io> aren't so much designed for compute-intense jobs so much
> as applications that are being accessed by lots of people at once and have
> to be scaled up to many small servers.

messages.body_plain:
If someone does talk to Michael or any of the lawyers in tech transfer office I'd be curious to hear a report back to the list.  While discussions among developers seem to focus on the distinction between GPL-style/copyleft and MIT-style/permissive licenses, much less discussed are the other differences between open source licenses, particularly with respect to perceived implications for patents.  For instance, my understanding from the tech transfer office here at Berkeley (who didn't elaborate much) is that they view GPL 3 as impermissible for externally distributed software, but are fine with GPL 2.  Other licenses, like Apache 2,0, (favored by many collaborators precisely because it is a permissive MIT style license that shows a bit more lawyerly awareness of these issues than MIT) finds itself in even more murky ground: according to them, UC is okay if you can redistribute Apache-licensed code in unmodified form, or modify it only to fix bugs, but not otherwise.  See this immensely confusing chart on modifying and re-distributing code under various open source licenses: https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/222586/24767439/cd58fc1c-1ab3-11e7-910c-432fbb6809cb.png

(A separate issue involves who are bound to these rules; e.g. staff face different copyright agreements wrt regents than faculty, but that is less important to me as it is of little help to have greater freedom as faculty member if staff are also contributing to the codebase anyway).

Thanks!

D-RUG,

As a followup, I asked about why you would use map() versus walk() on Twitter and got a couple of responses. To summarize, you can use print within map() to emulate a walk(), but one benefit of a walk() is that you get the input (.x or .) back afterwards.
https://twitter.com/bhive01/status/923958282967908352
Quite a few responses, but as I mentioned, I've not been able to realize this benefit in a meaningful way, but that is likely due to inexperience than anything else. The proposal I haven't made is to improve the documentation so that the examples showcase this benefit better.

Additionally, there was some question around why purrr::map() versus base::lapply() during the early parts. I hope I explained that they are effectually similar, but that due a few features and the wider family of map() functions map() was more consistent. If that wasn't clear, Hadley posted a thorough response to that exact question on SO detailing the benefits and costs of map.
https://stackoverflow.com/questions/45101045/why-use-purrrmap-instead-of-lapply/47123420#47123420

I hope that is helpful,

Brandon

Hi all,

I am attempting to use what looks like it should be a very straightforward package by Wolpert called acmeR. Our data have been vetted dozens of times, and cleaned, etc, and yet, we get some bizarre errors trying to run through many of our datasets for both bird and bat carcass searches conducted every 7- and 28-days over the course of a year. The data need to be in the following format:

“Date”,“Time”,“ID”,“Species”,“Event”,“Found”

“1/7/2011”,“08:00:00 PM”,“T091”,“UNBA”,“Place”,TRUE

“1/8/2011”,“12:00:00 PM”,“T091”,“UNBA”,“Check”,TRUE

“1/8/2011”,“16:00:00 PM”,“T091”,“UNBA”,“Search”,FALSE

(see vignette here, which describes this: https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/acmeR/vignettes/acmeR_Vignette.html)

Here is my data head:

      Date    Time Species      ID Event Found
10/17/2016 1:39 PM    VATH GHBT007     P     T
10/17/2016 2:26 PM    CORA GHBT004     P     T
10/17/2016 2:30 PM    EUST GHBT006     P     T
10/18/2016 6:43 AM    CORA GHBT004     S     T
10/18/2016 8:30 AM    EUST GHBT006     S     T
10/18/2016 9:40 AM    CORA GHBT004     C     T

I have tried editing date formats, event and found factor levels, etc. It doesn't make a difference in outputs/results. I have ordered the data chronologically, as the vignette advises.

Here are some of the errors, depending on subsets of the data, etc:
Error in solve.default(rv$hessian): system is computationally singular: reciprocal condition number = 1.57221e-20
In sqrt(diag(Sig)[2]) : NaNs produced
Error in solve.default(rv$hessian) : Lapack routine dgesv: system is exactly singular: U[2,2] = 0
In searching the interwebs, I have found nothing enlightening, and no bugs reported (well, no info) on acmeR, other than the vignette and some papers that don't go into too much detail, and don't explore errors. It seems a very straightforward package, and the data requirements seem very straightforward as well, but three different ecologists can't figure this out, so I am hoping UCD ecologists might have some insight or experience with this package!

Thank you in advance :)

So very unfortunately the long long long post I wrote about these calculations as detailed in the Wolpert paper has deleted itself. It's 22 pages, so I won't try writing a summary of that again, but basically it takes six variables into account:

Date of a carcass placement, search for a carcass, or check of the carcass.
Time of the above
(above should be ordered chronologically in the dataframe, which I have verified)
Species: arbitrary species codes
ID: unique carcass ID (a carcass might be placed out one time, and then checked/searched for 7-10 times within the year, so there can be about 10 rows per unique carcass, but each will have different dates/times/and potentially found info
Event: was this a carcass placement (P), a search for a carcass (S), or a check of the carcass (C)?
Found: was the carcass found? Yes (TRUE, or T), or No (FALSE, or F)

The system then uses these data to determine how long a carcass persists after placement, if it is found by the searcher or not, and how often it is found to determine carcass persistence/bleedthrough (was a carcass placed, searched for, and not found, but then found later on, aka "bleedthrough), searcher proficiency (how good are searchers at finding carcasses? Generally this diminishes over time because of scavenging, etc), and number of carcasses found versus how many were placed (as well as the species). This information is all determined with the function acme.summary().

The estimated parameters are then entered into acme.post <http://acme.post>, along with number of fatalities recorded, to come up with an estimated number of annual fatalities. However, I can't get past acme.summary without errors, and the carcass persistence estimates for subsets of data that I can get to run are, to say the least, ridiculous (e.g., 20,000+ days - no carcass stays out that long sitting on the top of the ground).

And yet, the data all look reasonable and correct. Nothing unusual that any of us can see.

OK, sorry.  Here are a couple more suggestions that you might or might
not find useful.

(1) Use the 's' command, rather than the 'n' command,  in the debugger
to step "into" the next line of code.  (You don't want to do that in
*all" cases.  Stepping into "lm", for instance, probably wouldn't be
fruitful.)

(2) See if you can stop the program *inside* the function, as:

> trace ("acme.summary", browser, at = 42)

Tracing function "acme.summary" in package "acmeR"
[1] "acme.summary"

See the "at" argument on the "trace" help page.

The idea would be set the breakpoint at various locations within the
code and then just let the code run.  If no error message has popped
up by line 42, then increase the line number to 84, let's say, and run
the code again.  If the error message does pop up, then quit and set
the breakpoint to, say, 63 and run again.  Lather, rinse, repeat until
you have identified the problem area.

Note, by the way, that you can download the code for the "acmeR" package from:

https://cran.r-project.org/src/contrib/acmeR_1.1.0.tar.gz

Looking at that might provide some insight.

I'm a bit embarrassed to offer all this gritty stuff, but I don't know
what else to tell you.  Maybe you can just ask the package maintainer:

Robert Wolpert <wolpert at stat.duke.edu <http://stat.duke.edu>>

for help if you haven't already done that.

Hi all,

I'm trying to extract y values for all integer values of x that are present on a smoothed plot. I have a plot of size vs age and I am trying to figure out what age individuals are at each whole number size. I've tried running the following code:

vonbertgrowth <- function(ta,t0,Linf,k){
  Lt <- data.frame(size = NA, age = NA)
  for (i in 1:ta){
    Lt[i,1] <- Linf * (1-exp(-k*(i-t0)))
  }
  Lt$age <- 1:ta
  return(Lt)
}

blueRockfish_vbg_f <- vonbertgrowth(ta=50,t0=-1.145,Linf=38.150142,k=0.172)

ggplot(data = blueRockfish_vbg_f, aes(y = age, x = size)) +
  geom_smooth()

smooth_vals <- predict(loess(blueRockfish_vbg_f$age ~ blueRockfish_vbg_f$size), data = blueRockfish_vbg_f)

It outputs the following plot:

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-MgLGLqmwooQ/WgyBSHMlM3I/AAAAAAAAAVo/tCgWHB1W5sIc_65C8ga6DRwP8AMaMfOFACLcBGAs/s1600/Size%2Bvs%2Bage.jpeg>

The problem is that smooth_vals ends up being a vector length of 50. Since size only goes up to ~48, I know that it isn't counting integer values of size. Additionally, when I change the input value of 'ta' for the vonbertgrowth() function, the length of smooth_vals changes to match. So I think that smooth_vals is predicting for integer values of age. How do I get it t predict for size?

Thanks for the help,
David

messages.subject_clean: error in grobs using grid.arrange
messages.body_plain:
Hi Corey,

I think the error you were getting was due to using grobs=c(test1, ...) rather than grobs=list(test1, ...) in grid.arrange. Here are a few examples using the built-in mtcars data frame:

# Create seven identical plots just for illustration
p1 = ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg)) +
    geom_point()
p2 = p3 = p4 = p5 = p6 = p7 = p1

# Put the plots in a list
plots = list(p1,p2,p3,p4,p5,p6,p7)

Now we can plot them like this:

grid.arrange(grobs=plots, layout_matrix=lay)

But if your plots are separate objects, you don't need to put them in a list. You can do either of the following instead:

grid.arrange(p1,p2,p3,p4,p5,p6,p7, layout_matrix=lay)
grid.arrange(grobs=mget(paste0("p",1:7)), layout_matrix=lay)

However, if you can generate your plots with a function that outputs a list of plots (either by iterating over groups in a data frame or iterating similar plots over a list of data frames), then you may be able to do your plotting with less code. Here's a toy example as the plots below would be better generated as a single plot with faceting:

plot.list = lapply(unique(mtcars$carb), function(group) {
  ggplot(mtcars[mtcars$carb==group, ], aes(wt, mpg)) +
    geom_point()
})

If your x and/or y axis variables are the same in each plot, then you can remove the x-axis and y-axis titles from the individual plots and substitute a single title for each axis like this:

grid.arrange(grobs=lapply(plot.list, function(p) {
  p + theme(axis.title=element_blank())
}), bottom="Weight", left="MPG", layout_matrix=lay)

Hope that helps.

Best Wishes,
Joel
